# Overview

This document describes the intended end state of the TRA pipeline: what it does,
not how. The pipeline starts from no data — a fresh project directory with no
downloaded filings and no firm list — and ends with a structured database of
every Tax Receivable Agreement disclosed on EDGAR, the public companies that
pertain to each one, and human-readable timelines at both the firm level and the
TRA level. The TRA-level timelines explicitly track contracts as they move
between companies via acquisition, spin-off, beneficiary reassignment, or
repurchase.

The pipeline is organized into five phases. Phases 1 through 4 run end-to-end on
the first build. Phase 5 is the incremental-refresh path that runs on a schedule
once the initial build is in place.

# Pipeline diagram

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
    A["EDGAR full‑text search"] --> B["Phase 1<br/>Discovery and acquisition"]
    B --> C["data/tra‑mentions/"]
    C --> D["Phase 2<br/>Per‑firm reading"]
    D --> E["Phase 3<br/>Cross‑firm consolidation"]
    E --> F1["Phase 4a<br/>Firm timelines"]
    E --> F2["Phase 4b<br/>TRA timelines"]
    E --> F3["Phase 4c<br/>Structured tables"]
    F1 --> G["Phase 5<br/>Refresh"]
    F2 --> G
    F3 --> G
    G -.->|new filings| A
```

# Phase 1: Discovery and acquisition

**Goal:** discover every TRA-mentioning filing on EDGAR and download the
relevant documents into per-firm directories.

A single EDGAR full-text search step returns per-filing hits across the variants
of "Tax Receivable Agreement", grouped by the filer's CIK. The same step filters
those hits to filings within the form types we care about (8-K, 10-K, 10-Q,
S-1, S-4, prospectus variants, proxy statements) and downloads the relevant
documents per firm. For each filing, the step saves:

- The primary document (the 8-K body, the 10-K body, the registration statement
  body, etc.) so the per-firm reading agent in the next phase can understand the
  business context — what transaction was happening, who the parties were,
  whether the TRA was being created, amended, terminated, or merely mentioned.
- Any EX-10.* exhibits that mention TRAs in the body. Exhibits that do not
  mention TRAs are skipped.

Filings whose only TRA mention is non-substantive boilerplate (negative-covenant
carve-outs, generic enumeration of "Indebtedness" types) are still downloaded
at this stage; the determination of whether the firm is a genuine TRA party
happens in Phase 2 with the agent reading the body.

The output is one directory per firm at `data/tra-mentions/<firm-slug>/`,
containing the firm's downloaded filings indexed by accession number. The phase
runs end-to-end on the first build, then incrementally during Phase 5 refresh
to catch new firms and new filings since the previous run.

**Deliverable:** a populated `data/tra-mentions/` tree with one subdirectory per
discovered firm.

# Phase 2: Per-firm reading

**Goal:** for each firm, read its filings in chronological order and write a
narrative log that explains what happened with the TRA at this company and
classifies each filing's TRA exhibits by operative effect.

For every firm directory, a dedicated agent reads the firm's filings one at a
time, oldest first, and appends an entry to that firm's `filing-log.md`. Each
entry explains:

- What this filing was about — what transaction or disclosure prompted it.
- Why the TRA is mentioned — whether the firm is establishing, amending,
  terminating, repurchasing, settling, or merely referencing a TRA in passing.
- The firm's role with respect to the TRA — whether it is the obligor (PubCo),
  a beneficiary, an acquirer that has assumed someone else's TRA, a financing
  arm, or a firm that mentioned a TRA without ever being a party to one.
- Which exhibits in this filing are themselves TRA-class documents — original
  contracts, amendments, restatements, terminations, repurchases, settlements,
  or assignments — versus exhibits that merely reference TRAs.

Each firm's `filing-log.md` carries a YAML frontmatter section that captures the
firm-level summary (firm name, CIK, TRA relevance, TRA role) plus a
machine-readable table of every TRA-class exhibit discovered across the firm's
filings, with the operative-effect description for each. The narrative explains
the story; the frontmatter and table make the file consumable by Phases 3 and 4.

This phase is where the agent does the work an automated regex classifier cannot
do: read the 8-K Item 1.01 body to see what the transaction is, follow the
chronology across filings to understand whether a 2024 termination is unwinding
a 2014 origination, recognize that an "Exchange and Termination Agreement"
attached to a merger 8-K is a TRA termination even though its title does not
contain the words "Tax Receivable Agreement". Section 11 of
`tra-background.md` documents the substance-over-form rule that the agent
applies.

The agent works one firm at a time, sequentially. The `filing-log.md` itself
serves as the agent's durable memory across long firm processing — when the
agent's context fills, prior filings' narrative entries are still in the log
and inform later decisions. The firm-level processing is independent across
firms, so parallelism is at the firm level.

**Deliverable:** one `filing-log.md` per firm, with frontmatter, narrative, and
machine-readable exhibit table.

# Phase 3: Cross-firm consolidation

**Goal:** group TRA-class exhibits across firms by underlying contract, so the
same contract appearing in multiple firms' filings is recognized as one
contract that has moved between parties.

A single TRA can appear under multiple CIKs over its lifetime:

- The originating PubCo files the original TRA in its IPO 8-K.
- An acquirer files the amendment or termination instrument when it buys the
  PubCo.
- A beneficiary discloses receipt of payments in its periodic filings even
  though it never filed the contract itself.
- A financing-arm subsidiary discloses related-party TRA-payment activity.

Phase 3 walks all firms' `filing-log.md` files and groups TRA exhibits by the
underlying contract. Two exhibits represent the same contract when their
parties, effective date, payment terms, tax attributes, and termination
provisions all match (Section 9 of `tra-background.md` carries the full
criteria). When the agent's reading in Phase 2 already established the
cross-CIK link (e.g., "this is the same TRA that originated at Acme PubCo and
was assumed by BigCo at the 2024 merger"), Phase 3 honors that link. When the
link is ambiguous, the consolidation step raises the case for manual review
rather than guessing.

The output is a contract-level index: one entry per distinct TRA, listing all
firms that have ever been parties to it, and all exhibits across all firms that
represent that contract in any state (original, amended, restated, terminated).

**Deliverable:** a TRA index identifying every distinct contract and its
cross-firm document set.

# Phase 4: Output generation

**Goal:** produce the three end-user deliverables — per-firm timelines, per-TRA
timelines, and the structured database.

This phase consumes the per-firm logs from Phase 2 and the cross-firm index from
Phase 3, then emits three artifacts.

## Per-firm timelines

For each firm, a concise chronological summary of its TRA-related activity:
which TRAs it is party to, in what role, with what payment activity, and how
its position with respect to each TRA evolved. A firm with one TRA that
originated at IPO and remained in force gets a short timeline; a firm that
originated a TRA, was acquired, had the TRA transferred to the acquirer, and
later disclosed beneficiary-side receipts gets a longer one.

The firm timeline answers: *what is this company's TRA story?*

## Per-TRA timelines

For each distinct TRA identified in Phase 3, a chronological summary of the
contract's lifecycle across all parties: origination, amendments, restatements,
beneficiary reassignments, acquirer assumption, terminations or repurchases.
When a TRA moves between firms (a beneficiary is acquired, an obligor merges
into another company), the per-TRA timeline tracks the contract through the
transition rather than fragmenting it across the per-firm views.

The TRA timeline answers: *what is this contract's story?*

## Structured database

The same information rendered in structured tables for downstream analytical
use. The tables are append-friendly so Phase 5 refreshes can extend them
without rewriting history. The minimum set:

- A TRA-level table: one row per distinct TRA, with originator, current
  obligor, beneficiary identity, key dates, current status, and the four
  standard contractual terms.
- An events table: one row per TRA event (origination, amendment, restatement,
  termination, repurchase, beneficiary change, acquirer assumption), with date
  and source-filing citation.
- A firm-TRA-role table: one row per (firm CIK, TRA id) pair, with the firm's
  role (PubCo, beneficiary, acquirer, financing arm, never-executed) and the
  date range over which it held that role.

**Deliverable:** per-firm timeline files, per-TRA timeline files, and the
structured database tables.

# Phase 5: Refresh

**Goal:** keep the database current as new filings appear on EDGAR over time,
without rebuilding from scratch.

The refresh path re-runs Phase 1 in incremental mode: query EDGAR for filings
filed since the previous run, identify any new firms that have begun mentioning
TRAs, download the new filings into the existing per-firm directories. For
firms with new filings, the Phase 2 reading agent picks up where it left off —
the existing `filing-log.md` provides the firm's history, and the agent
appends new entries for the new filings only.

Phases 3 and 4 then re-run against the updated logs to refresh the cross-firm
index and the output artifacts. When a refresh introduces a new TRA-relevant
event (a previously in-force TRA gets terminated, a new firm becomes a TRA
party for the first time), the timelines and database tables update accordingly.

**Deliverable:** an updated database state reflecting all EDGAR activity through
the refresh date.

# Order of skill / script invocation

The mapping from phases to project skills and scripts. Skill design and exact
script names may evolve; the conceptual order does not.

| Phase | Skill or script | Output |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Discovery and acquisition | `tra-download-filings` (refactored to query EDGAR for TRA-mentioning filings, group by CIK, download primary docs alongside TRA-mentioning EX-10s; no Query C). | `data/tra-mentions/<firm-slug>/` populated. |
| 2. Per-firm reading | A new per-firm reading skill that operates on one firm-slug directory at a time. | One `filing-log.md` per firm. |
| 3. Cross-firm consolidation | An aggregation script that reads every `filing-log.md` and produces a contract-level index. | TRA index. |
| 4a. HTML-to-markdown | `tra-htm-to-md` (converts TRA contract HTML to clean markdown for the human-readable timelines). | `.md` companion files for each contract. |
| 4b. Per-firm timelines | A timeline-build script that consumes firm logs and contract-level index. | Per-firm timeline files. |
| 4c. Per-TRA timelines | A timeline-build script that consumes the contract-level index. | Per-TRA timeline files. |
| 4d. Database tables | A database-build script that emits the structured tables. | TRA, events, and firm-TRA-roles tables. |
| 5. Refresh | A `tra-refresh` skill that orchestrates incremental re-runs of Phases 1 through 4. | Updated database state. |

# Out of scope for this document

This document is the conceptual end state. It does not specify:

- File formats, library choices, or data-engineering details. Those decisions
  live in the individual skill specifications.
- How the reading agent prompts are written, or what its decision rule is.
  Section 11 of `tra-background.md` carries the substance-over-form
  classification rule that the agent must apply.
- The exact CIK seed methodology, sampling decisions, or rate-limiting rules.
  Those live in the discovery and download skill specifications.
- Quality-assurance steps, manual-review interfaces, or how disagreements
  between the agent and a human reviewer are handled. Those belong in a
  separate quality-control document.

The goal here is to make the end-to-end flow legible so that every implementation
choice can be evaluated against whether it serves this flow.
